item.title: Binary Search
item.description: Binary search is short enough to memorize and subtle enough to keep producing bugs. Performance work magnifies both properties: removing one branch is useful only if the replacement still handles an empty range, duplicate keys, and the past-the-end answer. This chapter keeps one contract throughout. Given a sorted array a and a key x, lower_bound returns the first index i such that a[i] is not less than x. The answer belongs to the half-open set $[0,n+1)$: it is n when no such element exists, including when $n=0$.

item.title: Static B-Trees
item.description: The Eytzinger layout turns binary search into a walk through an implicit tree. A static B-tree applies the same idea with wider nodes: fetch a block of sorted keys, determine one child number, and discard several binary decisions at once. The word static matters. Without insertions or deletions, child positions can be derived from indices and nodes can be packed densely. A dynamic B-tree needs spare capacity, ownership, and explicit child references; that is the subject of the next chapter.

item.title: Search Trees
item.description: A static index can spend linear preprocessing time on a perfect layout. A search tree cannot: after every insertion it must still be searchable, balanced, owned, and within its allocation bounds. The natural continuation of the static B+ layout is therefore not “add a few pointers.” Updates introduce a larger contract: which keys are legal, and how duplicates are ordered; minimum and maximum node occupancy; who owns nodes and whether their addresses remain stable; how separator keys change after a child changes; what happens when the root splits; which iterator or pointer guarantees the container provides.

item.title: Segment Trees
item.description: Segment trees are a useful test of data-structure engineering because the asymptotic answer is known before optimization begins. Point updates and range reductions both take $O(\log n)$ time; the interesting questions are how many nodes are touched, how they are laid out, and which operation receives the simpler inner loop. We start with one precise interface over a zero-initialized array: add(i, delta) changes $a_i$ by delta; prefix_sum(k) returns the sum on the half-open range $[0,k)$; range_sum(l,r) returns the sum on $[l,r)$.

item.title: Tries
item.description: A comparison tree learns one bit of order at each branch. A trie consumes one symbol of the query. For a set of strings, this changes the natural complexity from “number of keys times comparison cost” to the length of the queried prefix. It also creates a hardware problem: the textbook implementation allocates one node per prefix and follows a dependent pointer for every byte. The asymptotic improvement can disappear into memory latency.

item.title: Range Minimum Query
item.description: The minimum of an array is easy to compute and impossible to undo. That second property is what makes static range-minimum queries unusually fast. Given an immutable array $a$, the range minimum query (RMQ) asks for $$ \min{a_l,a_{l+1},\ldots,a_{r-1}} $$ on a half-open interval $[l,r)$. We will build the array once and answer many queries. Updates belong to a different problem; a segment tree trades constant query time for $O(\log n)$ queries and updates.

item.title: Hash Tables
item.description: A hash table is often introduced as an array plus a clever formula that turns a key into an index. This description is mathematically sufficient and architecturally misleading. The hash function only chooses where a search begins. Performance is mostly determined by what happens after two keys choose the same place: how entries are laid out, how many unrelated bytes are fetched, which condition terminates a failed lookup, and what deletion leaves behind.

item.title: Bitmaps
item.description: Suppose we need to store a subset of the integers $0,1,\ldots,U-1$. A hash set stores the elements that are present. A bitmap stores one answer for every possible element: $$ B_i = [i \in S]. $$ This sounds wasteful until the universe is reasonably dense. Then the representation uses exactly $U$ bits, has no hashes or pointers, and answers membership with one indexed load. More importantly, one machine instruction can combine 64 membership answers at once.

item.title: Probabilistic Filters
item.description: Suppose checking whether a key exists requires a disk read, a network request, or a lookup in a much larger data structure. Most queries are misses. A small in-memory structure that rejects almost all of those misses can save much more time than it costs, even if it occasionally says “maybe” and forces an unnecessary lookup. This is an approximate membership filter. For a set $S$, it answers: definitely absent x is not in S possibly present x may or may not be in S The asymmetry is the point.
